items.title: What is GTA6 and why is everyone talking about it?
paras: Grand Theft Auto 6 is out this week and here is everything you need to know By Gianfranco Di Giovanni and Kyle Pauletto ABC Arts
Have you noticed that the gamers in your life have a new-found pep in their steps?
Is there an unusually large number of colleagues starting to come down with a nasty cough at the start of this week?
Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) is the latest in the long-running, critically acclaimed video game series by developers Rockstar Games.

GTA 6 is set in Leonida, a fictional, Florida-inspired state. The story follows two leads, Jason Duval, and Lucia Caminos, who is the first female playable character in the series since it first introduced fully fleshed out protagonists in GTA III in 2001.
The game puts players in the shoes of low-level criminals tasked with completing missions, building a reputation, and exploring a massive open-world map whilst unfolding a sprawling narrative.
At its core is the simulation and sandbox elements, the game contains lots of emergent or spontaneous gameplay moments, outside of the scripted single-player campaign.
Vice City, where this game is set, was a previous location of the fan favourite 1980s themed Grand Theft Auto: Vice City released in 2002.
The playable area in GTA 6 is roughly twice the size of previous title Grand Theft Auto V, sitting about 50 to 75 square kilometres.
Although that elevator pitch could be applied to many video games throughout the history of the medium, Grand Theft Auto has reigned supreme in the genre for more than 25 years.
Vice City is based on a fictionalised Miami and surrounding Leonida takes in the Florida Keys and the Everglades. ( Supplied: Rockstar Games )
Firstly, Rockstar's reputation in the industry carries a lot of weight due to its consistent output of mega hits.

The studio's last release, the open-world cowboy adventure Red Dead Redemption 2, took home Game of the Year at the Australian Games awards the year it was released, as well as four awards at the US Games Awards for Best Narrative, Best Score, Best Audio Design, and Best Performance for Roger Clark's voice work as one of the most beloved protagonists in modern media, Arthur Morgan.

Rockstar also has a reputation for pushing the technological boundaries of the medium, and fans got a taste of what's to come during a 30-minute extended look of GTA VI which premiered on Netflix earlier this year, which showed off the game's stunning photo-realistic visuals and cutting-edge physics engine in action.
Above all else though, the reason this entry in the series is so hotly anticipated is due to the incomprehensible success of the LAST entry.

Grand Theft Auto V (GTA 5) was a juggernaut, garnering widespread critical acclaim, record sales, and spawning an online multiplayer mode that resulted in the game continuing to be a bestseller for years after release. More than 230 million copies of GTA 5 have been sold in the 13 years since it first hit shelves.
GTA Online the multiplayer version of the game has been visited by millions of players, and has become an important part of the game experience outside of the single-player campaign.
Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos are the dual protagonists of Grand Theft Auto VI. ( Supplied: Rockstar Games )

The GTA series has left a trail of controversy behind it, and has long been criticised over its depiction of violence and crime, particularly here in Australia where in 2014 GTA 5 was pulled from Kmart and Target shelves after a Change.org petition amassed more than 47,000 signatures.

Now in 2026, the conversation around violence in video games has quieted, but in its place are accusations of AI usage in development, hackers leaking gameplay vision years ahead of release, and claims of poor working conditions inside the studio.

But the most prominent controversy so far came in June of this year, when Rockstar announced that copies of GTA 6 bought from physical stores would not include a game disc, just a digital download code. This outraged many people, from physical media purists to those who just prefer to wait for cheaper pre-owned copies to hit shelves.

The issue reached its peak when a hacking group called CyberLeek began release footage it had obtained of the near finished product, threatening to leak more if Rockstar didn't change its policy on physical game discs. Although this was initially claimed as an act of consumer rights activism, it was soon revealed that a crypto-scam element was a main motivator for the group.

GTA 6 has been classified R18+ by the Australian Classification Board, meaning it is legally restricted to adults aged 18 and over due to the games depictions of high-impact violence, sex scenes and drug use.
Despite a lot kids wanting to play this game, it's definitely aimed and only for adult players.
The download size of the game is more than 200 gigabyte and has been available for pre-loading ahead of the launch since last week.
On the PlayStation 5, the installed size will be approximately 212GB and on Xbox Series X|S it will be about 234GB.

According to a support post on the Rockstar Games site, GTA 6 will be available at midnight local time on November 19, 2026, which means Australian and New Zealand players will be some of the first in the world to play the game.
If you live in Melbourne it also means you'll be playing three hours earlier than those living in Perth, sorry sandgropers.
Just like on New Year's Eve, those keen gamers in Kirimati on the island nation of Kiribati however will get to play a full three hours earlier than anyone in mainland Australia.
Rockstar has said it needed the extra months to finish the game to the standard it wanted. It first promised the game for 2025, then moved it to May 26, 2026, and finally to November 19, 2026.

The delays carried significant commercial weight, and not just for Rockstar, with other developers moving the release dates of upcoming games to avoid clashing with what is expected to be a massive release.

If you were thinking about "chucking a sickie" to visit Leonida, you might want to book in some annual leave, as the Fair Work Ombudsman helpfully pointed out that most other types of leave aren't likely to hold up if you're questioned.

items.title: British actor Robert Pattinson named as new James Bond
paras: British actor Robert Pattinson will succeed Daniel Craig as the next James Bond. ( Reuters: Isabel Infantes )
The 40-year-old actor, whose recent films include The Odyssey and Dune: Part 3, has described being cast in the role as a "dream come true".
Oscar-nominated filmmaker Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next film in the multi-billion-dollar 007 franchise.
British actor Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond, Amazon MGM Studios has announced, taking one of cinema's most coveted roles.

The Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm, his tailored tuxedos and a fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history.
The franchise made its debut in 1962 and the movies have brought in more than $US7 billion ($10.3 billion) in global ticket sales since Sean Connery brought Agent 007 to the big screen in Dr No.

More than two dozen Bond films have been released. The upcoming movie will be the first Bond adventure under Amazon MGM Studios, which took creative control of the film franchise under a new joint venture with longtime rights holders Michael Wilson and Barbara Broccoli in 2025.
Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the Dune trilogy and Arrival, is set to direct the new film, with a script written by Briton Steven Knight.

Pattinson, who has already had a busy 2026 with films The Odyssey, The Drama and Primetime and who will also feature in Villeneuve's Dune: Part Three, to be released next month, succeeds Daniel Craig, who bowed out of the Bond role after the 2021 movie No Time to Die.
"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement.

"I'm deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me," he said, referring to producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman and executive producer Tanya Lapointe.
"I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."
Pattinson, 40, made his big-screen debut in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in 2005 and has gone on to star in films such as The Twilight Saga, The Lost City of Z and Tenet.
Robert Pattinson with his Twilight Saga co-stars Kristen Stewart and Taylor Lautner in 2011. ( AP: Matt Sayles )
He is no stranger to following other actors to play famous characters, having taken on the lead role of the famed caped crusader in 2022 film The Batman.
Pattinson only recently joined a list of reported contenders for the James Bond role that included the likes of Slow Horses actor Jack Lowden and One Night Only star Callum Turner.
Villeneuve said Pattinson has "the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new".
The Bond series is based on novels by Ian Fleming. His first book, Casino Royale, was published in 1953.
Other actors who played Bond include Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton and Pierce Brosnan. George Lazenby played the character in one movie, 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service.
The official Instagram account of Britain's royal family welcomed the news, saying: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."
"Few films carry the kind of anticipation that comes with James Bond, and we have strived to honour the passionate fans, the legacy, and the future of this iconic character.

"We are thrilled to officially welcome Robert Pattinson as our 007 and are confident he will bring something truly special to this role. Robert, Denis, Amy, David, and Tanya are embarking on an amazing adventure together."

items.title: Tame Impala and Baz Luhrmann earn Grammy nods as Raye leads nominations
paras: Raye leads the 2027 Grammy Award nominations, with 11 including for record, song and album of the year. ( Reuters: Eduardo Munoz )
British singer Raye, the artist behind Where Is My Husband, tops the list of Grammy Award nominees with 11.
Australian artists recognised include Tame Impala who is up for Record of the Year for Dracula, a collaboration with Jennie.
The 2027 Grammys will take place on Sunday, February 7, US time, in Los Angeles.
The nominees for the 2027 Grammy Awards have been announced from New York's Time Square, with Raye leading the way.
The British singer earned 11 nods including for song and record of the year for Where Is My Husband and for album of the year for This Music May Contain Hope.
Spanish musician Rosalía racked up nine nominations, days after she dominated the Latin Grammys with her album Lux.
Among the Australian artists to be nominated were Tame Impala, including for record of the year, and Baz Luhrmann for Epic: Elvis Presley in Concert.
Dolly Parton, the country music legend who died in August, received three posthumous nominations.
The 2027 Grammys will take place on the evening of Sunday, February 7th (the morning of Monday 8th, Australia time), in Los Angeles.
Aussie band Tame Impala have been recognised for their single Dracula, with Jennie.

items.title: Netanyahu rival demands probe into PM's office over election fraud claims
paras: Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker PM until a new coalition government is established. ( Reuters: Ronen Zvulun )
Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, is demanding an investigation into the Israeli Prime Minister's Office amid allegations it may have fabricated claims of electoral fraud.
Mr Netanyahu and his Likud party have been claiming the election was "stolen".
Mr Eisenkot is currently steering negotiations to form a new coalition government, following Israel's inconclusive election on October 27.
Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival is demanding an investigation into the Israeli Prime Minister's Office, following explosive allegations it may have fabricated claims of electoral fraud.
Gadi Eisenkot, who is currently steering negotiations to form a new coalition government, said Mr Netanyahu posed "a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy".

For weeks since Israel's inconclusive election on October 27, Mr Netanyahu and his Likud party have been claiming the election was "stolen", describing the surge in support for Arab-Israeli parties at the ballot box as illegitimate and the result of voters being paid off.

On Sunday night, Israel's Channel 12 reported that the prime minister's chief of staff, Ido Norden had contacted the Israeli police commissioner's office with a complaint about members of the United Arab List (UAL), the party often referred to as Ra'am in Hebrew.
The network said Mr Norden's source was actually a former employee of the Prime Minister's Office.

The intervention led to the homes of three UAL members being raided on the morning of the election without search warrants and the men arrested on allegations of electoral fraud, after envelopes of cash were discovered.
Mr Netanyahu used the arrests to ramp up his rhetoric on election day, accusing Arab-Israeli or Palestinian-Israelis of trying to steal the election.
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, gives a thumbs up following the exit polls at his party headquarters, on the evening of Israel's national election. ( Reuters: Shir Torem )

It has also been reported that the head of Israeli intelligence agency Shin Bet, David Zini, tried to wire-tap three members of the other Arab-Israeli party, the Joint List ahead of the election amid suspicion of foreign interference in the poll.
His request was denied by Israel's Attorney-General, a public servant and the country's legal advisor, and his agency failed to provide more evidence to back up the demand.
Reports have also suggested Mr Zini, who was hand-picked to be Shin Bet chief by Mr Netanyahu, wanted some Arab-Israeli politicians arrested on election day.
The Netanyahu government has been highly critical of the Attorney-General, Gali Baharav-Miara, relentless accusing her of blocking its agenda.
Gadi Eisenkot said the affair was further reason why Mr Netanyahu should not "remain at the helm of government for even one more minute".
"Under no circumstances must Israel be dragged into another election with him as prime minister.
"It is clear that as long as he remains in office, Israel can no longer expect elections that are fair and lawful."

Another member of Mr Eisenkot's Yashar party, former Shin Bet director Yoram Cohen, wrote to the Attorney-General on Monday, local time, demanding a criminal investigation into whether the police and intelligence agencies were being used by Mr Netanyahu to undermine the election.
"The fear that the state's enforcement powers were used to advance political interests in the midst of election day requires a thorough, independent and impartial investigation," Mr Cohen wrote.
Former prime minister Yair Lapid described the situation as an "orchestrated" attempt by Mr Netanyahu's office and his Likud party to steal the election.
"As more and more details come to light, it becomes clear," he posted on X.
"This wasn't an attempt to disrupt the elections. It was an attempted coup."
Likud described Mr Eisenkot's comments as "outrageous incitement" and "appalling".
"While the prime minister extends a hand for unity, Eisenkot and his colleagues issue inflammatory, incendiary statements every day in venomous language," it said.
"Eisenkot is inciting against the chief of staff, a law-abiding citizen who passed information to the police about suspicions of a serious criminal offence, as he was obligated to do."
The United Arab List and the Joint List secured 19 out of the 120 seats in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset.

Israel Police has confirmed an internal investigation is underway, with the force's deputy commissioner looking at "all systemic, organisational and command-related aspects concerning the allegations made against Israel Police".

"It should be emphasised that all police actions, including the activity carried out on the morning of election day, were conducted with a commitment to transparency and accountability to the public, and with the aim of safeguarding the integrity of the elections," a spokesperson said in a statement.
Ido Norden, Mr Netanyahu's chief of staff, has threatened Channel 12 with a defamation suit worth 2.5 million shekels (1.14 million AUD).
Mr Norden's lawyers claimed threats had been made against his life since the report went to air.

"[The report] constitutes an act of fraud on a national scale, masquerading as "journalistic work," and represents a new and dangerous low in the contamination of public democratic discourse in Israel.

"Your decision to disseminate these baseless, false claims—along with malicious lies—in the midst of an investigation into the conduct of the elections, is intended solely to exert an improper and unlawful influence on the outcome of the elections in Israel."

items.title: Six people arrested in cross-border drugs smuggling network: ED
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) linked to a cross-border drugs smuggling network . An investigation by the Directorate of Enforcement ( ED ) unearthed a major drug trafficking operation involving the smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India. Lovejit Singh alias Labba , Manjeet Singh alias Manna were arrested on October 11 while Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh and Ramandeep Singh were arrested on October 18 and one Gurpreet Singh was held on October 20, the agency said in a statement. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons ie Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi. They were were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder.

According to the central probe agency the accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs. According to ED , the investigation under PMLA linked to a cross-border drugs smuggling network was initiated based on the seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by DRI and the seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 Kg. of heroin has been seized so far. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where the identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. The accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in the local market. Further, the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles in the second-hand market for trafficking from the storage hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri Madhya Pradesh, and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Previously, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits were attached by the ED . (ANI)

items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "India matters most for future of planet" says British High Commissioner Lindy Cameron
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): In recent times when climate change has become a pressing issue with countries across the world being ravaged due to climate catastrophes, it becomes imperative to discuss and deliberate upon global actions that can help the world rise up and meet these challenges. At the NDTV World Summit's a discussion was held on the theme, "India Matters The Most For Future Of Planet". Participants in the discussion included Erik Solheim, Former Minister of Climate and the Environment of Norway; Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India; Shishir Priyadarshi, President Chintan Research Foundation; Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. "India is the country that matters the most for the future of the planet and climate change. India's ambition for development should not in any way be constrained by the responsibilities of the planet," Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India, emphasised. She noted that the UK is committed towards the Multilateral Development Banks (MDB) reforms, technology and research support in India to aid the efforts. "Every dollar invested in resilient infrastructure pays 4 times over," said Cameron. "Lived experience of climate emergencies helps people to understand why their government needs to take policy action now," she added. Further talking about the need for urgent government action, Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said, "Series of disasters affecting both developed and developing countries are serving as a wake-up call. As rich countries will get more and more affected by climate change which they did not imagine till a couple of years ago, most vulnerable countries are going to be struggling with impacts who also have very less capacity to deal with it. India is taking a leadership role in the global fight against climate change. Initiatives such as Global Biofuels Alliance, International Solar Alliance, and Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure are some efforts taken by India in recent years to manage the climate crisis. (ANI)

items.title: India to grow at 6.8 pc in FY25 and 6.6 pc in FY26: S&P Global Market Intelligence
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): India's growth, although moderating, remains strong with a forecasted average of 6.8 per cent for the fiscal year 2024-25 and 6.6 per cent for 2025-26, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence . Despite a slowdown in economic momentum due to weaker public-sector investment, the outlook for India's economy is buoyed by several positive factors. Easing inflation, favourable monsoon conditions, and increased government social spending are expected to boost household demand. Additionally, healthy corporate balance sheets are playing a vital role in supporting the recovery of private investment. S&P Global Market Intelligence has released its October Global Economic Forecast update, emphasizing a steady global economic expansion supported by policy stimulus, while acknowledging risks from geopolitical factors. The outlook highlights moderating inflation and easing monetary policies as key factors steering the global economy towards a "soft landing."

Ken Wattret, global economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence , remarked, "The global economy is on track for a soft landing, with inflation rates moderating and monetary policy easing becoming more widespread. Still, geopolitical developments have the capacity to dampen or even derail the expansion." Report forecasts an annual real GDP growth rate of 4.3 per cent in 2024 and 4.4 per cent in 2025 for the region excluding China and Japan. Aiding this growth is resilient domestic demand, as regional central banks adopt more accommodative monetary stances. The start of the US Federal Reserve's easing cycle in September is creating more room for interest rate cuts, prompting several central banks, including those in the Philippines, New Zealand, Hong Kong SAR, and Indonesia, to lower rates. S&P Global Market Intelligence underscores that while the global economic outlook remains positive, risks persist. Geopolitical tensions could potentially derail economic progress, especially in regions with heightened uncertainties. Nonetheless, policy measures aimed at stimulating growth, coupled with moderating inflation, are setting the stage for a sustained economic expansion. (ANI)

items.title: How I used evidence and imagination to write an account of the world in 2096
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print Fatih Aktas/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images How do you invent the future? This isn’t a question that I had ever had to consider until I set out to imagine what the world would be like in 70 years’ time for New Scientist ’s 70th anniversary. As a lifelong sci-fi nerd, I have read and watched loads of material that could have served as inspiration. But this being New Scientist , I wanted to make sure that I was as grounded in real science and technology as possible – while acknowledging that no prediction of the future is ever correct.

I began by asking my colleagues on the magazine for their ideas about the future and then attempted to corral this sci-fi smorgasbord into something resembling an outline of a self-consistent narrative. Part of the problem in imagining many different futures is that they contradict themselves – you can’t have the war-torn AI dystopia of Terminator alongside the utopia of Star Trek .

I wanted both hope and realism in my future, so I decided to look at how the scientific literature handles the end of the century. One of the most obvious forecasts is for climate change, where we have a pretty good idea about what might happen in 2096, under a range of scenarios, because it all boils down to atmospheric physics that we can model. Of course, which of these scenarios we end up with is all too dependent on human politics, so the science alone couldn’t guide me. I also turned to population projections , which, for the most part, are locked in based on current population trends. The idea that the end of the century will be the first time we are living in a world of falling populations became a fascinating strand in the final piece.

The biggest problem I faced was how to deal with AI. I am not confident making predictions on this topic even just a few years in advance – as I’ve written previously, my views on AI have evolved between the release of ChatGPT in 2022 and now , so how could I possibly predict what would happen by the time we got to 2096? Furthermore, there was a risk that AI could come to dominate the piece, crowding out everything else. There is a graph I often think about, published by the Financial Times under the headline “AI could end scarcity, end humanity – or boost [GDP] growth by 0.2 percentage points”. I knew that, to preserve any meaningful narrative, I had to restrict AI to this boring middle option, so I invented an AI-fuelled financial crisis that would see us place limits on the technology. I have no idea if such an event is likely to happen, but it seems to me to be the only way to preserve a future that remains comprehensible to us today.

I spoke to dozens of experts to help inform this piece, expecting them to contradict each other in ways that were both helpful and confounding, and they did. But what I found most interesting is how little interdisciplinary forecasting there is across science. For example, attempts to predict future public health trends are only just starting to consider how climate change will interact with the diseases and medical conditions we face. Meanwhile, many of the people I spoke to hadn’t deeply considered how AI would affect the evolution of their chosen discipline.

In weaving all this together, one of the most surprising things I arrived at was the idea of expanding the legal concept of personhood. Looking at how our attitudes towards both animals and artificial intelligence are changing today, it seemed to me that this was a possibility, so I created the International Treaty on Non-Human Personhood. Its existence in the story had a number of interesting downstream effects, and I kept finding different ways for non-human people to influence the world. Again, this is a big bet, but I think not an unreasonable one.

One thing I couldn’t escape from in writing this piece is the idea that I and probably all of the people I interviewed won’t be around to see what comes to pass. I would be 110 years old in 2096 – not impossible, especially given the advances in medicine I describe in the piece, but still unlikely. In some ways, 70 years from now is the perfect amount of time to forecast the future, being just outside most adults’ expected lifespan. We can never know what will really happen – we can only imagine.

items.title: Nuclear bomb in space would disable 98 per cent of satellites within a week
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print Nuclear weapons were tested frequently in the 20th century, but a detonation in space today could be devastating Sipa/Shutterstock A single nuclear explosion in space would wipe out 98 per cent of satellites within a week, sending vital technology around the world into disarray from which it would take years to recover, warn experts.

Zachary Petersen at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and his colleagues modelled the effect of a 1 megaton explosion 500 kilometres above the South Atlantic. They found that an initial spike of X-rays from the blast was damaging, but it wasn’t the most disruptive part: electrons released by radioactive fission would become trapped in Earth’s magnetic field, exposing satellites to a kind of artificial radiation belt, over and over again.

This level of exposure would take out 98 per cent of satellites within one week. And while many spacecraft use specialised computer chips that are more resistant to radiation , the researchers found that even when they altered their simulations to assume that satellites were three times more resilient to radiation damage, the effects were still disastrous, with 97 per cent still failing within two weeks.

Worryingly, such explosions aren’t without precedent. The US detonated a 1.4 megaton nuclear bomb at an altitude of 400 km in 1962 . Satellites were disrupted by the blast, but Earth was orbited by only a relatively small number of devices at the time – humans have now launched around 25,000 objects into space , many of which still orbit the planet. Global navigation systems like GPS, internet connections and weather forecasts rely on these satellites and the data they provide.

A nuclear explosion in space would probably have long-lasting repercussions, not only because satellites would need to be replaced, but because there would be an estimated 20 collisions within two years as broken satellites drifted aimlessly. Those collisions present a risk of Kessler syndrome, a theoretical scenario in which debris hits other satellites, creating more debris and a chain reaction of destruction that would make orbit lethal to future launches for decades, or even longer.

The Outer Space Treaty now bans the launch of nuclear weapons into space, and all major spacefaring nations are party to it. But tensions remain. In 2024 a vote was raised at the UN to reaffirm commitment to the rule, which Russia vetoed . Earlier that year, the US had warned that Russia plans to launch a space weapon with possible nuclear capabilities .

Petersen and his colleagues didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, but Craig Underwood at the University of Surrey, UK, says the consequences of losing so many of our satellites would be catastrophic for society because we are so dependent on space technology.

“The recent low-Earth orbit mega constellations [like Starlink] would be particularly affected,” says Underwood. “During the Cold War, much thought was given to protecting critical space systems and our societies were much less dependent on electronic technology. I suspect that since the 1990s, less attention has been paid to the prospect of having to survive a nuclear conflict. Our civil defence infrastructure has been dismantled, and society is much more vulnerable.”

“While individual satellites can, in principle, be replaced relatively quickly, recovery would not be straightforward. New satellites would have to be launched into an environment still affected by elevated radiation levels and increased debris, potentially limiting their operational lifetime and effectiveness. As a result, restoring orbital infrastructure could take years,” says Chantal Cappelletti at the University of Nottingham, UK. “The result would not be an immediate collapse of modern society, but rather a prolonged degradation of many services that we now take for granted. Recovery would likely require years of rebuilding orbital infrastructure while managing elevated radiation and debris hazards.”

items.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
paras: MIT Technology Review The Big Story Artificial intelligence Biotech & health Climate & energy 10 Breakthrough Technologies AI Hype Index The Impossible issue Menu MIT Technology Review MIT Technology Review The Big Story Artificial intelligence Biotech & health Climate & energy 10 Breakthrough Technologies AI Hype Index The Impossible issue Sponsored
While we’re used to predictable technology, AI challenges that assumption. Therefore, the goal must be bounded, observable, and controllable AI.

In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.

Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.

Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.

With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.

Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.

It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.

Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.

The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.
Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:

The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

Tiafoe is the lowest-ranked player in the Ivan Lendl Group, which also features Daniil Medvedev and Flavio Cobolli. He didn’t secure his spot in the event until earlier this month, becoming the second-to-last player to do so after Rafael Jodar.

“It’s a great experience to be out here. It’s kind of weird coming out and playing your first match against him. It was fun, about the whole hour of it, was a lot of fun [smiling]. But yeah, I mean, it’s a great experience to be out here,” Tiafoe , who made his ATP Finals debut, said during his post-match press conference on Sunday.

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
